content.title: How GSMC is Advancing Gender-Responsive Media in East Africa
content.summary: GSMC has trained over 200 journalists across East Africa in gender-responsive reporting, equipping them with tools to challenge bias and drive more just, inclusive, and representative storytelling.

media.alt: How GSMC is Advancing Gender-Responsive Media in East Africa

content.text: The Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications (AKU-GSMC) took a bold step of mainstreaming gender reporting in newsrooms by delivering a series of gender training in East Africa.

Seven Gender-Responsive Reporting and Communication Continuous Professional Development (CPD) trainings were conducted in Nairobi, Meru, Kisumu, Kampala, Mwanza, and Dar es Salaam. More than 200 journalists were trained and these weren't just about skills upgrade, but were also about justice, voice, and visibility.

The decision to roll out these trainings was informed by a clear and urgent gap: gender representation in media remains unequal, stereotyped, and biased. Women and marginalised groups are often either invisible or portrayed in reductive ways. Part of the challenge is that many journalists and communication professionals have not been trained on how to challenge these narratives.
AKU-GSMC's goal was clear: to strengthen capacity, inspire reflection, and spark change within media ecosystems that too often reinforce inequality.

The trainings were facilitated by fellows from GSMC's own gender training of trainers (ToT) programme, media professionals who had previously undergone intensive instruction in gender-responsive communication. Their transition from learners to facilitators shows what sustainable change looks like: training that does not just teach but multiply impact.

Each training session offered a safe space for honest dialogue, creative problem-solving, and deep reflection. Participants explored how gender bias appears in headlines, sourcing, imagery, and framing, and how these patterns affect the public's understanding of issues like politics, health, education, and conflict. Across borders and contexts, the same truth echoed: media must do better, and media professionals are ready to lead that change.

During the final session in Dar es Salaam, the impact of this work was undeniable. From Kenya to Uganda to Tanzania, a growing network of gender-aware communicators has been set up. Through these trainings, AKU-GSMC has reaffirmed its role not only as a hub of learning but as a regional leader in advancing equity, ethical journalism, and the power of inclusive storytelling. The work continues, but these seven trainings have laid a foundation that will shape East African media for years to come.
